name: Alphonso Mango
short_description: Export-grade Hapus from Ratnagiri and Devgad. 200–350 g, fibreless saffron flesh, shipped at 12–13 °C in ventilated 3 kg and 5 kg trays.
long_description: Alphonso, called Hapus in Maharashtra, is the mango most importers ask for by name. Fruit from the Ratnagiri and Devgad belt on the Konkan coast carries a thin skin, almost no fibre, and a saffron-orange flesh that holds its aroma through a three-week sea passage. Laterite soil and sea air are the reason the same variety grown inland does not eat the same way, and buyers in the Gulf and the UK grade on it.

We pick at 80–85% maturity for sea freight and at 85–90% for air, based on specific gravity and shoulder fill rather than calendar date. Fruit moves from orchard to the pack house within six hours, is washed, hot-water treated where the destination requires it, graded by weight into 200–250 g, 250–300 g and 300–350 g counts, and pre-cooled before it goes into the reefer.

Vapour heat treatment and hot water treatment are both available for markets that mandate them, and every consignment is residue-tested against EU MRL limits before dispatch. Buyers taking their first container usually start with a mixed count 3 kg box, which retails well and reduces ripening variance on arrival.

name: Bhagwa Pomegranate
short_description: Deep-red Bhagwa from Solapur and Sangola. Two bahars give near year-round supply, 45–60 day shelf life at 4–5 °C, 3.2 kg and 4 kg cartons.
long_description: Bhagwa is the variety that made Indian pomegranate exportable at scale: a hard, glossy, deep-red rind that travels, soft seeds, and arils that hold colour for weeks. It outsells older varieties like Ganesh in every destination we ship to, and Solapur, Sangola and Nashik between them account for most of the export-grade crop.

Two flowering cycles matter for planning. Mrig Bahar fruit ships August to February and carries the deepest colour; Hasta Bahar covers February to May and bridges the gap before the next cycle. Between the two we can quote a buyer almost year-round, which is the reason importers hold Bhagwa on contract rather than spot.

Fruit is graded on weight into 200–250 g, 250–300 g and 300 g-plus, sleeved in EPE net to stop rind scuffing, and pre-cooled to 5 °C before stuffing. Sun-scald, cracking and aril browning are the three defects that cost a buyer money on arrival, so each is checked on a sample from every pallet at the pre-shipment stage.

packing: 3.2 kg or 4 kg CFB carton with EPE net sleeves and corner cushions

packing_note: Cartons are stacked five high on a pallet with corner posts, strapped and shrink-netted. Buyer-specified carton print and PLU stickers are available from 2,000 cartons.

name: Thompson Seedless Grapes
short_description: Nashik and Sangli Thompson Seedless at 16+ Brix, 16–18 mm berries. GLOBALG.A.P. and GRASP certified, SO2 pads, 45–60 days at 0–2 °C.
long_description: Thompson Seedless is India's highest-volume table grape export and the one European retailers audit hardest. Nashik and Sangli ship from January to April, which lands in the window between the Southern Hemisphere and Mediterranean crops, and that timing is why Dutch and British programmes hold Indian volume every year.

Bunches are field-graded, trimmed of loose and undersized berries, and moved to a pre-cooling chamber within four hours of cutting. Sulphur dioxide pads go in at packing to hold botrytis for the full transit, with the pad type matched to whether the box is punnet-packed or loose.

Because retail programmes drive this product, we work to the buyer's specification rather than a house standard: berry size, bunch weight, punnet format and label are all set before the first container. GLOBALG.A.P. with the GRASP social module is in place at farm level and the certificate travels with the documents.
packing: 4.5 kg punnet box (10 × 500 g) or 8.2 kg loose, with SO2 pad and perforated liner

name: Cavendish Banana (Grand Naine G9)
short_description: Green mature G9 hands, 6–9 inch length and 32–42 mm girth, in 13.5 kg telescopic cartons. Year-round supply, 21–28 days green life at 13.5 °C.
long_description: Grand Naine, sold as G9, is the Cavendish clone that carries almost all of India's banana export volume. It ships green and mature, ripens predictably in the destination chamber, and holds a uniform hand shape that retailers can merchandise without sorting. Gujarat, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu together give us fruit in every month of the year.

Green life is the number that decides whether a container arrives sellable. We cut at 75–80% grade, de-hand and wash in the field pack house, treat the crowns, and get fruit into a 13.5 °C reefer within a day of cutting. Below 13 °C the fruit chills and greys; above 14.5 °C it starts ripening in transit, so the reefer set point is checked and logged at stuffing.

Middle East programmes take the bulk of this product on repeat monthly volumes. For those buyers we hold fixed hand-count specifications and a standing carton print, so a repeat order needs a quantity and a vessel, nothing more.

name: Fresh Kagzi Lime
short_description: Thin-skinned acid lime, 35–55 mm, dark green and high in juice. Year-round with a June–October peak, 10 kg and 15 kg cartons or mesh bags.
long_description: Kagzi lime is the small, thin-skinned acid lime that Gulf buyers use for fresh juice and food service. The name means paper-skinned, and that thinness is the point: juice recovery runs well above what a thicker-rind lime gives, which is what a juice bar or a catering kitchen is actually buying.

Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra carry fruit through the whole year, with the heaviest and best-coloured crop between June and October. Off-peak fruit runs slightly paler and we say so at quotation rather than at arrival.

Fruit is washed, waxed where the destination allows it, graded to 35–45 mm and 45–55 mm, and shipped at 9–10 °C. Below 8 °C limes take chilling injury and pit, so the reefer is set conservatively and the set point is recorded on the stuffing report.
variety: Kagzi acid lime · 35–45 mm and 45–55 mm
packing: 10 kg or 15 kg CFB carton, or 20 kg ventilated mesh bag
payment_terms: LC at sight, or 30% TT advance with balance against B/L copy
packing_note: Mesh bags cost less per kilo and suit wholesale markets; cartons protect better for retail and long transits. We will recommend one over the other for your route rather than quoting whichever is cheaper.
